title: The Alapin Sicilian
description: An easy setup against the Sicilian Defense. Played even at Grandmaster level, but especially effective under 1800 elo.

3rk1nr/pp2bppp/2n5/q2p4/3N4/2N4P/PP2QPP1.text:
After the bishop blocks, Black has the same problems as in the main line. 

We will increase pressure with Nb5, Re1 and Bg5. White is better.

3rkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/q2P3b/8/2N2N1P/PP2BP.text:
Placing the rook on the d-file to pin the pawn is tricky. 

However, our idea is development plus the basic Nd4 idea for the check on e2.

First we will ensure our king safety. Then we can go for tactics.

3rkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/q2p3b/8/2N2N1P/PP2BPP1.text:
After Black takes, we don't care about a pawn. Nd4 opens up lines.

We want to focus on the king. 

12...Bg6 fails due to 13.Bb5 and suddenly that e-file is cleared for the rook!

3rkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/q2p4/3N4/2N4P/PP2bPP1/.text:
This is the best move, but it allows us e-file play.

We'll take back with check.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/2n5/3q4/3Pp3/2B2N2/PP3PP.text:
This continuation is quite common and logical.

But logical and straightforward continuations aren't necessarily okay. 

We'll push the knight into e5 and play for the advantage.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/2n5/3qp3/1b1P4/2N2N2/PP3.text:
This pin is the only move that doesn't lose.

But after we unpin, Black will have to give us the bishop pair.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/2n5/3qp3/3P4/2b2N2/PP1B1.text:
The bishop takes.

We'll recapture with the bishop. 

This is the most active move.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/8/3qn3/3Pp3/2B5/PP3PPP/R.text:
This capture, for example, is quite natural. But it's bad!

After we recapture, the e5-pawn is a beast on that square.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/8/4P3/4p3/2B5/PP3PPP/3RK.text:
But we control the d-file and the d6- and f6-squares. 

Bc4 and Rd6 are great ways to continue, and a great plan is to castle and place the rook on e1 to attack e4. White is again borderline winning.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3q4/3P4/2N2N2/PP3.text:
d5 is coming. 

Black is losing. d5, Bf4, Nb5. This should be easy.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3q4/3P4/5N2/PP3PP.text: To show you how things can go wrong for Black, even natural development is bad.

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3q4/3P4/8/PP3PPP/RN.text:
Black can recapture and attack the d4-pawn. 

Black has two developed pieces, so they are quite active.

Before we gain a tempo, we have to defend the d-pawn.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/3qp3/3P4/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
This is a risky way for Black to play.

I like attacking the queen while developing here.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP1P1P.text:
Nc6, developing, is the most popular move. It is played 35% of times. 

It covers the d4 square somewhat, but we can still push with d4. And we will!

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3pP3/2P5/PP3PPP/.text:
Black usually plays this trade.

So let's just recapture.

Now we have two strong central pawns! 

Not bad!

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3p4/3PP3/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
This is the most popular move, being played over 2 million times. 

Black wants to challenge our central pawns.

We'll just take here, and gain some tempi on the queen.

r2qkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/7b/3P4/1QN2N1P/PP2B.text:
And d5 is pretty much guaranteed. 

White will be pretty comfortable in a middlegame if this move is played because they'll have virtually zero weaknesses. 

Black on the other hand is still down in development.

r2qkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/8/3P2b1/2N2N2/PP2BP.text:
I suppose many players could go for this, which reminds me of a Qd8 Scandinavian.

We'll kick the bishop back. White enjoys a stable edge and may even play for d5 to get rid of the IQP.

r3k1nr/p3bppp/2p5/q2p4/8/2N4P/PP2QPP1/R1.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll castle. Our rook is coming to e1.

r3k1nr/pp2bppp/2n5/q2p4/3N4/2N4P/PP2QPP1.text:
The bishop blocks, but this is a pin.

Just taking is fine here. 

We remove a defender of the e7-bishop.

r3k1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3q4/1b1P2b1/2N2N2/PP.text:
This one is by far the most popular. 

Black pins the knight.

Castling here rekindles the threat of Nxd5.

r3k1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3q4/3P2b1/2b2N2/PP2B.text:
Black doesn't have to take the knight, but they often do.

This trade favors us because we no longer have an IQP after recapturing.

r3k2r/p2qnppp/1pn1p3/8/2PP2b1/5N2/P3BPPP.text:
The queen goes to d7.

And Ba3 is still a great move here. 

If Black castles, they'll be in a pin.

r3k2r/p3bppp/2p2n2/q2p2B1/8/2N4P/PP2QPP1.text:
Black's best move is 15...Kf8. 

We have won the opening battle and have denied Black the luxury of castling.

r3k2r/p3bppp/2p2n2/q2p4/8/2N4P/PP2QPP1/R.text: The nice thing about taking on c6 is that once the g8-knight comes out, only the king defends e7.

r3k2r/p3nppp/1pn1p3/3q4/3P2b1/2P2N2/P3BP.text:
Black usually plays their pawn up.

But we can begin attacking the queen, with c4.

r3k2r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/3q4/3P2b1/2P2N2/P3BP.text:
To cover those dark squares, many players will get their knight on e7. 

Ba3 doesn't prevent ...0-0 anymore.

But the b-file is still weak and White has a semi-open file to attack on.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3q4/3P2b1/2P2N2/P3BP.text: After 10...Nf6, Black may think they're ready to castle.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3q4/3P2b1/B1P2N2/P3B.text:
But we can control the e7- and f8-squares.

We'll also be attacking Black if they castle on the queenside. 

Moves like Rb1 and Qb3 (if Black moves their queen away from d5) will be great for b-file pressure.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3q4/3P2b1/2N2N2/PP2.text: But we develop with that nice tempo on the queen.

r3kbnr/p3pppp/2p5/8/3q4/8/PP3PPP/RNBQK2R.text: Without the knight's defense, the queen is hanging.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3q4/3P2b1/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
This pin is actually quite challenging.

We'll break the pin and defend.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3q4/3P4/5b2/PP2BPPP/R.text:
This is not how chess works. 

We get a free tempo when we recapture.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/8/3q4/5B2/PP3PPP/RNBQ.text:
This blunder runs into the tactic of removing the defender. Black should retreat and accept they've miscalculated.

We'll take on c6 with check.

r3kbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3q4/3P2b1/5N2/PP2BPP.text:
Since 7...Bxf3 achieves nothing, 7...e6 for normal development is best.

We should attack the queen here with Nc3. 

Black has a few options.

r3kbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/q6b/3P4/2N2N1P/PP2BP.text:
They usually do not do so.

But d5 is free here. 

You shouldn't be concerned about the d-file.

r3kbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/q7/3P2b1/2N2N2/PP2BP.text:
The queen on a5 pins the knight.

Now h3 is a useful move to see if Black bites and takes on f3.

r3kbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/q2p3b/8/2N2N1P/PP2BPP1.text:
If Black takes, this is exactly what we wanted. 

The main idea behind d5 is not to recapture right away. 

We want to play this discovered attack.

r3kbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/q2p4/3N4/2N4P/PP2bPP1/.text: Black captures on e2, but in doing so, they bring our queen to the open file.

r4rk1/p2qnppp/1pn1p3/3P4/2P3b1/B4N2/P3BP.text:
There isn't a good way to deal with the pressure. If the knight moves to a5, Ne5 comes. 

The engine even thinks that giving up the exchange is the best idea by going for mass trades on d5.

All of this thanks to a more mobile center thanks to our early 2. c3 move.

r4rk1/p2qnppp/1pn1p3/8/2PP2b1/B4N2/P3BPP.text: So if Black castles for instance, d5 wins.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The Sicilian Defense.

And now we play c3. 

The main idea is to play d4. 

In addition, we want to get Black out of their theory!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to a course on another reliable weapon against the Sicilian, the Alapin Variation! 

This variation consists of playing c3 on move two. 

In this first study, we'll go over the most popular fourth move for Black, which is 4...d5, and I'll teach you how to achieve good positions!

We begin with 1. e4.

r1bq1r2/pp2nppk/2n1p3/3pP3/1b1P4/2N2N2/P.text:
Black may as well take.

And after the knight check, all legal moves lose.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npp1/2n1p3/3pP1NQ/1b1P4/2N5/.text: White gets a powerfully winning attack following the themes of the Greek Gift Sacrifice.

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/2n1p3/3pP3/1b1P4/2NB1N2.text:
And this is a common blunder, walking into our idea.

Now Bxh7+ works!

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3pP3/1b1P4/5N2/PP3.text:
For example, many players go for 6...Bb4+, looking for quick development. 

But we can just block with the knight.

Black never wants to capture on c3. 

They would have too many dark-squared weaknesses and White's structure wouldn't be bad.

r1bqk2r/pp2b1p1/3ppnn1/4P2p/5P1P/2NB1N2/.text:
And this should be the end. 

White will win material.

r1bqk2r/pp2b1p1/3ppnn1/7p/4PP1P/2NB1N2/P.text: The natural ...h5 to prevent h5 from White allows a discovered attack.

r1bqk2r/pp2b1pp/3ppnn1/8/4PP2/2NB1N2/PP4.text:
Black may think they'll be fine if they castle and develop. 

But they have a problem with the kingside knights!

Here comes the h-pawn! 

White's moves are just easy and natural to find, while Black must play accurately to stay alive.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/3pP3/1b1P4/2N2N2/P.text:
Black's idea was to get the bishop out and then the knight out through e7. 

Their problem now is that they cannot castle because of a common tactic.

8. Bd3 sets up the Greek Gift.

r1bqkb1r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/3pP3/3P4/5N2/PP3P.text:
This is the correct approach. 

The bishop achieves nothing on b4.

Once again, we should just get the knight out and develop.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1nn1/3P4/4PP2/5N2/PP4.text:
Black develops their knight. 

Developing poses Black many problems: basically, e5 is a big threat now and it is hard to deal with.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3pPn2/3P4/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black's entire plan is to attack d4. 

To defend it, I suggest we go for an a3 configuration because it will help us play Na4 if Qb6.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/3ppnn1/3P4/4PP2/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black may now challenge the center.

Taking is great for our structure. 

...Bxe6 is a blunder, so fxe6 is necessary.

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/3ppnn1/8/4PP2/2N2N2/PP4PP.text:
And after this trade, there's no need to go for anything forcing just yet.

We don't need to rush. Development is the most important thing. We'll develop our bishop.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/8/3PP3/8/PP3PPP/.text:
A move we should take seriously is 4...e6, played 27% of the time.

Objectively, it's not bad. Pushing 5. d5 doesn't give White a big advantage because Black can capture (5...exd5). So ...e6 does prove to be useful.

Therefore we'll simply develop.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP1P1P.text:
Nc6, developing, is the most popular move. 

It does control the d4-square, but we can still push the pawn.

And so we will!

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3pP3/2P5/PP3PPP/.text:
Black usually trades here.

We'll recapture and maintain two strong central pawns.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/8/3PP3/8/PP3PPP/RN.text:
As a testament to people's lack of preparation, 4...d6 is a mistake already and it has been played more than 450,000 times at the amateur level.

After d5 we are already better.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p2n1/3P4/4PP2/8/PP4PP/.text:
The knight retreats.

We should develop following normal opening principles. It's difficult for Black to untangle with this much less space.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/3Pn3/4P3/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
The most popular move is the worse one in this case. 

The knight is an easy target and we can get an advantage after chasing the knight with f4, gaining space.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3p4/3PP3/5N2/PP3PP.text:
The most natural continuation after ...e6 is ...d5. 

But we have a great game after simply pushing our e-pawn.

This is a good advanced French Defense, where we are in complete control of the center and the f6-square. 

Black has to develop both kingside pieces, which isn't so easy.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1pp1/2n1p3/3pPn1p/1P1P3P/P1N.text:
I like the option of expanding on the queenside. 

We control many more squares and create the b2-square for our bishop. 

If ...Qb6, Na4. We has a slight edge because of the extra space.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1pp1/2n1p3/3pPn1p/3P3P/P1N2N.text:
Black should stop this. 

But if they do, that's perfectly fine.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2n1p3/3pPn2/3P4/P1N2N2/.text:
d7 is the only square to develop the bishop to. 

As White, you cannot play Bd3 yet because of the pressure on d4.

Therefore I like 9.h4. The threat is to remove the knight from its outpost.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/3P4/2B1P3/2N2N1P.text:
And so do we. 

I like White's space advantage. This is what the Alapin is meant to give you if your opponents don't respond in the best way. 

We can play moves like Re1, Be3 and a4 to gain space. This is advantageous according to the engine, but there isn't a concrete way forward. We'll focus on piece placement and maybe play for f4 later on.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/3P4/4P3/2N2N1P/PP.text:
Black fianchettoes.

c4 is a good square for our bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/3P4/4P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
Because the pawns impede the bishop's movement you may see ...g6 for Black to develop it.

I like to control the g4-square with h3. 

That way we make it harder for Black to develop.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/3P4/4P3/2N5/PP3PP.text:
Since ...d6 protects the e5-square, people may go for ...Nf6.

We should continue with our development with Nf3.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The Sicilian Defense.

And now we'll play c3. 

The main idea is to play d4. 

In addition, we want to get Black out of their theory!

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/3P4/4P3/8/PP3PPP/RN.text:
This move is less popular but it causes less harm in Black's position.

There's no f4 with a tempo, so we should just develop naturally with Nc3.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Our analysis of 2...Nc6 continues with 2 moves that are less popular: 

...e6 and ...d6 on move 4. 

These setups seek to control Black's half of the center, but our pawns can still find a way forward.

We'll begin with 1.e4.

r1bqk2r/1p2ppbp/p1np1np1/1B1P4/4P3/2N2N2.text:
Black may try to attack the bishop and force it off the diagonal.

But we'll just retreat the bishop and induce Black to weaken themselves.

r1bqk2r/4ppbp/p1Pp1np1/8/Q3P3/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
And this should be a comfortable win. 

You're going to want to go for Bg5, 0-0 and Rac1 to support the c-pawn.

r1bqk2r/4ppbp/p1np1np1/1p1P4/B3P3/2N2N2/.text:
Black's point is that they break the pin, but in the process they lose a very important pawn.

We'll simply capture the knight.

r1bqk2r/pp1nppbp/3p1np1/1B2P3/3P4/2N2N2/.text:
At this point, 8. e5 is practically winning. Black's knights are in a tangle.

There's even a strong plan of e6 to weaken the pawns!

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/1B6/3PP3/2N2N2/P.text:
This is a more basic type of blunder. 

It's a self-pin on a vulnerable square.

d5 begs to be played!

r2q1rk1/pp1bppbp/2n3p1/1B2P3/5Bn1/2N2N2/.text: It's not easy to deal with this. White is completely winning.
If Black castles now, we can make use of the open d-file.

r2qk2r/pp1bppbp/2n3p1/1B2P3/5Bn1/2N2N2/P.text:
10...Nc6 looks normal, too.

But our main idea stands true: we will play Qe2, holding on to e5 and getting ready for h3.

r2qkb1r/pp1npp1p/3p2p1/1B1Pn3/4P3/2N1Q2P.text:
f4 is coming. 

Black has to find a way to untangle or they'll lose a piece!

If a6, your bishop goes to e2 and you're better because of the bishop pair and extra space.

r2qkb1r/pp1npp1p/3p2p1/1B1Pn3/4P3/2N2Q1P.text: If they block with the f-knight, we have a strong idea against the e5-knight.

r2qkb1r/pp2pp1p/2np1np1/8/3PP3/2N2Q1P/PP.text:
If they develop and attack our pawn, d5 is strong.

This is the nice thing about having a strong and mobile pawn duo in the center.

r2qkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/3Pn3/4P3/2N2Q1P/P.text:
Even though Black can centralize and attack our queen, it's just a tempo. 

It doesn't change the long-term aspects of the position. One of these aspects is that we have more space and central control.

It is good to insert this check. 

Black will have to ponder what knight they'll block with.

rn1q1rk1/pp1bppbp/6p1/1B2P3/5Bn1/2N2N2/P.text:
This move is natural, and so is Nc6. 

But against this all we have to do is attack the knight.

h3 pushes it to the edge of the board.

rn1q1rk1/pp1bppbp/6pn/1B2P3/5B2/2N2N1P/P.text:
On h6 it still has the f5-square, but we don't need to have tunnel vision with g4 stuff at this moment.

We should trade on d7 first.

rn1q1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/1b2P3/5Bn1/2N2N1P/P.text:
Black could always insert this capture.

Nevertheless, exchanging queens leaves us with a winning advantage...

rn1qk2r/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/1B6/3PP3/2N2N2/P.text:
If the bishop blocks...

We can start using our mobile center!

rn1qk2r/pp1bppbp/5np1/1B2p3/3P4/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black may trade, but we have another pawn that can take its place.

We'll recapture and attack the knight. 

Black's position is crumbling.

rn1qk2r/pp1bppbp/6p1/1B2P3/6n1/2N2N2/PP3.text:
The knight and bishop attack e5.

So we'll develop and defend the pawn.

rn1qk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1Pp1/1b6/3P4/2N2N2/PP3.text: We have a strong in-between move, winning a piece.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3PP1b1/2N2N2/P.text:
You may also see this pin.

But it isn't effective at all. 

Black is offering the bishop pair, in essence.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3PP3/2N2b1P/PP.text:
Taking is the most logical.

We should of course recapture.

rn1r2k1/pp2ppbp/6p1/1N2P3/5Bn1/5N1P/PP3P.text:
And we threaten Nc7 as well as hxg4. 

White is winning.

rn3rk1/pp1qppbp/6pn/4P3/5B2/2N2N1P/PP3PP.text:
After this recapture, what you'll often see is a queen trade.

First we'll castle, though. 

There's no need to initiate the trade.

rn3rk1/pp2ppbp/6pn/4P3/5B2/2N2N1P/PP3PP1.text:
It's hard for Black to make any progress. 

In fact, if they continue with Nc6, we've got Rd7. Rd7 is hard to stop and we'll attack everything on their 7th rank. This is winning, too.
If Black does trade queens, the game simplifies in our favor.

rnbk1b1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP3PPP/.text: With the king misplaced, this should be an easy to play middlegame.

rnbk1b1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2p5/4P3/2PB4/PP3PPP.text:
We can just go ahead and defend our pawn. 

We're a lot better after simple moves like Nf3 and 0-0.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3PP3/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
Black usually fianchettoes.

We'll develop with check and a tempo.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3PP3/2N5/PP3PP.text:
People usually continue with g6.

Against this, I suggest we just respond with normal development, achieving a classical central formation with our knights and pawns.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2p5/3PP3/2P5/PP3P.text:
I suppose we could explore what to play against this knight move. 

It's been played more than 25,000 times on the database.

I like taking on c5. It's the most practical try and Black is prone to blunder against it.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/8/3PP3/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
Black develops and attacks e4.

We'll develop and defend the pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p4/2P5/4n3/2P5/PP3PPP/.text: For example, they may think this is a good capture.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p4/2P5/Q3n3/2P5/PP3PPP.text: But this loses a knight for free.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP3PPP/.text:
Taking on c5 isn't good at all.

We can trade queens and make Black lose castling rights.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The Sicilian Defense.

And now c3 is the Alapin.

The main idea is to play d4. 

In addition, we want to get Black out of their theory!

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP1P1PP.text:
2...d6 is the second most popular move.

It is played 20% of times at the amateur level in over 2.5 million games in the database.

Let's play d4 when we are allowed!

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pq4/3P4/N1P2N2/P.text:
Black can develop and put pressure on d4.

We'll threaten a fork on c7!

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/n3pn2/1N6/3N1B2/2P5/PP3P.text:
But quite simply White is dominating with the active minor pieces aiming at the queenside. 

Nd6 will be a great move to play after Be2 and 0-0.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/1NP5/8/2P2N2/PP3P.text:
We don't mind the queen trade because at the end the c7-square is still a problem for Black. 

Black's going to have to defend!

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/1Np5/3P4/2P2N2/PP.text: Black is in some trouble here.

r3k2r/pp2bppp/2n1p3/2Pn3b/8/2P1BN1P/PP2B.text:
Since our bishop defends c5, Black attacks it, trying to undermine the defense of c5.

We'll play b4, holding on to the pawn.

r3k2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/2P4b/8/2P1BN1P/PP2B.text:
This trade of queens leads to an endgame in which Black needs to know what they're doing.

White recaptures, with d-file control.

r3k2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/2pq3b/3P4/2P1BN1P/P.text:
The bishop is developed to e7.

The pawn capture on c5 leads to a good endgame for us, but it also sets up a trap.

10...Bxc5 loses the bishop to 11.Qxd5 and the bishop loses its defender.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/2n1pb2/2Pn3b/1P6/2P1BN1P/P3.text:
Black targets c3, and also the b4-pawn, via the pin on the diagonal.

This is why we'll push our b-pawn, seeing as it is being attacked anyway.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/4p1b1/1PP3P1/1n6/2n1BN1P/P2.text:
And we'll defend our second rank. 

It will be important for us to play Ne5 and even Nc4 to maneuver. A trade with Nxe2+ is likely. 

That trade is of no concern: it gets rid of one of Black's most active pieces, and we can play our rook to b2 to attack the knight on b4.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/4p1b1/1PPn2P1/1n6/2b1BN1P/P.text:
The correct move is 15...Bxc3. Nothing fancy, just going for the pawn.

We'll just recapture with the knight.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/4pPb1/1PP5/1n6/4BN1P/P3nP2/.text:
Even though this move is check, the knight will come under attack.

We'll play Kf1. Now both the knight and the g-pawn are en prise.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/4pPb1/1PP5/8/4BN1P/P1n1KP2/.text:
But that would only win an exchange, not a full rook. 

We will take on g7 and play the strong Bg5 followed by Bf6. White is winning.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/4pPb1/1PP5/8/4BN1P/P1n1nP2/.text: Sure, Black can go after the rook in the corner.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/4pb2/1PPn3b/1n6/2P1BN1P/P3B.text:
When the knight goes to b4, we have a forcing line that sets up yet another opening trap for our opponents to deal with.

Step one is to attack the bishop on h5.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/4pbb1/1PP3P1/1n6/2n1BN1P/P3.text:
This is the little trap we set up. 

It looks like Black has a lot of activity.

But it all becomes illusory once we take the bishop.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/4pbb1/1PPn2P1/1n6/2P1BN1P/P.text:
Now we attack Black's other bishop! 

This is where Black could go wrong.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/4pbb1/1PPn4/1n4P1/2P1BN1P/P.text:
The bishop is forced away.

Now we'll attack Black's other bishop with g5! 

This is where Black could go wrong.

r3kb1r/pp1qpppp/2n2n2/2pP1b2/2P5/5N2/PP2.text:
But we can attack the knight right away. 

We'll likely see 8...Nb4. 9. Na3 is a good response, but the engine says that 9. 0-0 Nc2 is possible. 

The point is that we will have moves like Ne5 followed by g4 to attack the c2-knight's defender.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pq1b2/3P4/2P2N2/PP.text:
If Black develops without ...e6, we can push.

We'll play c4, getting ready to play d5.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pq3b/3P4/2P2N1P/PP.text:
That's why Black often doesn't capture.

At this point I like defending the d4-pawn with Be3.

cxd4 will allow us to recapture with the pawn and then put our knight on c3.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pq4/3P2b1/2P2N2/PP.text:
If pressure is applied on d4, we don't have to worry about the pawn just yet.

8. h3 is a useful move to insert. 

If Bxf3, we'll recapture and attack the queen and knight behind it.

rbb1k2r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/1NP5/2P1q3/5N2/PP2.text:
This is winning for us. 

Black is down a pawn with no compensation. 

The bishop on b8 is also bad. That's not the proper square for it and the rooks won't be easily connected.

rbb1k2r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/1Np5/2PPq3/5N2/PP2.text: Once it goes back to b8, we can win a pawn and threaten a check on d6.

rn2kb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pq4/3P2b1/2P2N2/PP3.text:
Players love going for this pin: it's very popular.

But Be2, gaining a tempo on the queen should minor pieces be exchanged on f3, is an effective solution.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pq4/3P2b1/2P2N2/PP2.text:
e6, to activate the f8-bishop, is often played.

We'll castle.

rnb1kb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/2pq4/3P4/N1P2N2/PP.text: We'll play Nc4, and threaten a fork on b6.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pq4/3P4/2P5/PP3PPP.text:
Here, Black can ignore the pawn and develop.

We'll just develop with Nf3.

In Study 1, we saw a similar position where we played Nf3, but in that study ...e6 had been played.

5...cxd4 is a transposition to 4...cxd4, as seen in Study 1.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/1N6/3q4/2P2N2/PP3PP.text:
Black accepts.

We'll recapture and have two really active knights.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pq4/3P4/2P2N2/PP3P.text:
With 5...e6, Black wants to develop their dark-squared bishop.

I like 6. Na3, intending Nb5.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/3q4/3p4/N1P2N2/PP3P.text:
6...cxd4 allows us play, too.

We'll bring the knight to b5 and threaten a fork on c7.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pq4/8/2P5/PP1P1PPP/R.text:
And after the queen recaptures...

We will play our d4 anyway.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/1N6/3p4/2P2N2/PP3PP.text:
The queen defends.

We'll propose a queen trade to remove the defender.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black goes for the Sicilian.

And we'll go for the Alapin.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/4P3/2P5/PP1P1PPP.text:
Black breaks in the center with 2...d5. 

They don't want to suffer with a lack of space, so they expand in the center.

Here we should capture.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this second study, I want to show you a challenging line. 

I'm talking about 2...d5 and 4...Nf6, two solid moves that combined could pose some problems.

We'll begin with 1.e4.

n2k1b1r/pp2pppp/4b3/4p3/8/5N2/PP3PPP/R1B.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll go after the bishop which is Black's only developed piece.

n2k1b1r/pp2pppp/8/4p1N1/2b5/8/PP3PPP/R1B.text:
But now it's only a matter of technique. 

If you know your Alapin well, this is the kind of win you can get!

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1n2n3/1N2p3/8/1B3N2/PP3.text:
11...Ne6 defends c7 for one move.

But we can remove the defender.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/2nq4/3p4/3N4/2P5/PP3PPP/R.text: Once the queen recaptures, we can develop our other knight.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/2nq4/3p4/3N4/N1P5/PP3PPP/.text:
We're going to play a middlegame following the classic principles of playing against the IQP. 

We want to blockade the pawn, trade pieces whenever possible (but not Nxc6 because we fix Black's structure).

r1bnkb1r/pp2pppp/1n6/4p3/8/1BN2N2/PP3PPP.text:
If the knight takes, e5 isn't defended, but we're not going after the pawn.

We'll play Nb5. We're going for the rook!

r1bq1rk1/pp1p1ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/1b6/1BN2NB1.text:
And we can place our bishop on a safer square. 

I really like the idea of getting a knight to d6. It will be a monster  on that square. The only thing that could alter our plan is ...Bxc3, but even then we have other ideas. 

Bc2 to target h7 for example.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pbppp/2n5/3pP3/3p1B2/2P2N2/P.text:
Black castles.

And we can capture, centralizing our knight. 

It's also a blockader of those doubled d-pawns.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2np4/3pP3/3N1B2/2P5/PP3.text:
Black should probably play d6. 

The idea is to get rid of the doubled pawns and lessen our central control.

We have to take.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/1nnbp3/8/8/1BN2N2/PP2QPP.text:
And we can pin the bishop on d6. 

...Qc7 is a trivial mistake because you get Nb5, a fork. 

So you'll probably see 12...Qe7. A nice plan is to go Bg5 to induce the f6 weakness and bring the bishop to e3. You have good compensation for the pawn!

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2nb4/3p4/3N1B2/2P5/PP3PP.text:
Black recaptures.

And since trading pieces is good when playing against the IQP, we shouldn't mind trading bishops.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/1b3B2/1BN2N2.text:
The bishop can pin our knight, but this isn't optimal development in the Alapin.

We can just castle because we are not troubled by ...Bxc3.

r1bqk2r/pp1pbppp/2n5/3pP3/3p4/2P2N2/PP3P.text:
Black could continue with simple development.

We should develop and defend e5.

If Black instead plays 8...dxc3, that helps us develop with 9.Nxc3.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/3b4/3pN3/3p4/2P5/PP3PPP/R.text:
The bishop goes to d6 because Black wants to castle soon.

But since our knight is on e5, Qa4+ is quite effective.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/3p4/1BP2N2/.text:
7...e6 by itself causes no harm to Black. 

As long as Black plays ...d6 or ...d5 later on, this move is fine.

We can take on d4 and strengthen the pawn on e5.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/8/1BN2N2/PP.text:
There's one major drawback to ...e6. The d6-square is weakened.

If we reinforce our central pawn, we make it harder for Black to play ...d6.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/3nP3/2Bp4/2P2N2/.text:
Some players could defend the knight with the pawn, thinking that they're fine with the trade because they get the bishop pair.

We can capture on d5.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n5/3pP3/3p4/2P2N2/PP3.text:
Black recaptures.

And we can castle kingside.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/1nn5/4P3/2Bp4/2P2N2/PP.text:
The option you'll see the most is probably Nb6 to attack your bishop.

We should just put it on b3. 

Black now has three options.

7...d5 and 7...d6 are essentially the same because you would take on d6 in both scenarios. We'll consider them in Study 4.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/1nn5/4P3/8/1Bp2N2/PP3P.text:
The most obvious is to grab the pawn.

We can recapture with our knight and develop.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n5/3nP3/3p4/2P2N2/PP3.text:
5...Nc6 is a logical move to develop a piece and pressure the center.

Attacking the knight with the bishop is a great idea. 

We don't care about recapturing on d4 right away.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/4p3/8/1BN2N2/PP3PP.text:
Black should not take this, although I am sure many people will!

The queen trade is winning. 

If the king takes the queen, f7 can be attacked with Ng5.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/1nnp4/4P3/8/1BN2N2/PP3P.text:
Black could undermine our e5-pawn.

It's possible to ignore e5 and just castle. 

There are tactics in the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/8/1B3N2/PP2QP.text:
We can just recapture. 

We want to castle and play a rook to our c- and d-files. The bishop's safest square for now would probably be d2. We have a slight edge thanks to the e5-pawn!

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/1nn1p3/4p3/3P4/1B3N2/PP2.text: This trade can happen, and it probably should for Black's sake.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/1nnpp3/4P3/3P4/1B3N2/PP3.text:
After 8...d6 to undermine our structure, we want to avoid queen trades.

And we want to support the e5-pawn, so we'll play Qe2.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n5/3pp3/3p1B2/2P2N2/PP3.text:
Black takes.

And we'll recapture with the bishop so that if there's a further trade we end up with a knight on e5.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2np4/3pP3/3p4/2P2N2/PP3P.text:
Black could also try undermining our e5-pawn.

We should defend e5.

r2k1b1r/ppN1pppp/1n2b3/4p3/8/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
The king goes to d8.

We'll take the rook.

r2qk2r/pp1b1ppp/3b4/3pN3/Q2p4/2P5/PP3PPP.text:
We're inducing the bishop to d7 and we can trade it off.

We'll take on d7.

r3k2r/pp1q1ppp/3b4/3p4/Q2p4/2P5/PP3PPP/R.text:
The queen recaptures.

Now Re1 forces Black into a self-pin.

r3k2r/pp1qbppp/8/3p4/3Q4/2P5/PP3PPP/RN2R.text:
But now material is equal and we have some activity. 

We want to play Nd2 to f3 and Re1 to double up rooks on the e-file.

r3k2r/pp1qbppp/8/3p4/Q2p4/2P5/PP3PPP/RN2.text: Black has to block it with the bishop.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1n2b3/1N2p3/8/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
The bishop recaptures.

We'll give a check, forking the king and rook.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/1n1bp3/8/8/1BN2N2/PP3PPP.text:
Black castles as well. 

And now it's time to make use of our d-file.

We'll shift the queen to e2, in preparation for Rd1.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/1n1bp3/8/8/1BN2N2/PP3PPP/.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop. 

But we have quick development.

Since there's no tension between the queens, we can castle.

We don't want a trade of queens since we want activity.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/1n2p3/4P3/2Bp4/2P2N2/P.text:
A very natural reaction is to play the knight to b6 and attack the bishop. 

This will allow Black to go up a pawn.

We'll retreat the bishop, accepting that Black can take on c3. We don't mind because we will have a lead in development.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/4p3/3nP3/3p4/2P2N2/PP3.text:
Black could also choose to support the knight in the center.

We'll develop and start applying some pressure to the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP1P1P.text:
The move 2...Nf6 is the most popular move in the games of titled players. 

However, under 2000 it is played in only 8% of games.

Now e5 is our most challenging continuation. 

We attack the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2pnP3/8/2P5/PP1P1PPP.text:
3...Ne4 gets the knight trapped with 4. d3, so Nd5 is best. 

But now we can strengthen the center.

We'll play d4 and connect our pawns.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/3nP3/3p4/2P5/PP3PPP/.text:
Black takes on d4. 

We won't recapture back right away.

The d-pawn is pinned, so we'll develop a piece with Nf3.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/1n2p3/3pP3/8/1BN2N2/PP3P.text:
Let's focus on 8...d5. 

This is the correct move and it isn't too hard to find.

Our approach will be to capture en passant to break apart Black's central formation. 

We don't want to allow them a strong pawn chain.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3p4/3pP3/3p4/2P2N2/PP3PP.text:
When they recapture, they temporarily have tripled pawns. 

Of course, they'll solve this issue soon.

We should support the e5-pawn with the bishop because our pieces will be active in the center.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3pp3/3nP3/2Bp4/2P2N2/PP3.text:
Black could choose to undermine the e-pawn. 

This allows us the trade on d5.

This is a good idea because it wrecks Black's structure.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/8/3pB3/3p4/2P2N2/PP3PPP/.text:
We'll castle soon. 

If 9...dxc3, 10. Nxc3 will give us three developed minor pieces to Black's zero. We should have a nice middlegame due to our activity, with pressure on the central d5-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/8/3pp3/3p1B2/2P2N2/PP3PP.text: If Black takes, we can just recapture.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black goes for the Sicilian.

We'll play c3 and go for the Alapin.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
The third study of Chapter 3 will cover 2...Nf6, which is also an important second move to go through.

The main idea is that Black attacks the e4-pawn quickly and takes advantage of the fact that we can't play Nc3.

Let's begin with 1.e4.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/8/3p4/1BP2N2/PP3P.text:
The queen recaptures.

Castling is our main idea. 

We do permit ...dxc3, but this shouldn't be an issue thanks to our development lead after Nxc3.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1nnqp3/8/3P4/1B3N2/PP3PP.text:
We should just capture and get ready to play Bg5. 

All our pieces are coming out and if Black isn't careful we'll achieve the d5-pawn push. Otherwise, we'll just play a standard IQP position, avoiding piece trades and getting a knight to e5.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1nnqp3/8/3p4/1BP2N2/PP3P.text: 9...e6 serves to enable the development of the f8-bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/1nn5/4P3/2Bp4/2P2N2/PP.text:
The option you'll see the most is probably Nb6 to attack the bishop.

We should just retreat it to b3.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n5/3nP3/3p4/2P2N2/PP3.text:
5...Nc6 is a logical move to develop a piece and pressure the center.

Attacking the knight with Bc4 is a great idea. 

We don't care about recapturing on d4 right away.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/3pP3/3p4/1BP2N2/PP.text:
...d5 and ...d6 are now equivalent moves, in the sense that we will capture the pawn either way.

After d5, we will take en passant to get rid of the strong d-pawn.

Our ideas still have to do with quick development.

r1q1kb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/1N6/5B2/1Qp2N2/PP3.text:
And we're forcing our way to the c7-square.

All thanks to offering material in exchange for development.

r3kb1r/pp1qpppp/1nn5/1N6/8/1Qp2N2/PP3PPP.text:
If something like 12...Qb8, Ng5 attacks f7. But this move has drawbacks too.

We'll bring our rook to the d-file with tempo.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/8/3p2b1/1BP2N2/PP3P.text:
This move is a pin on our knight, but we have a clever tactic.

We'll capture on f7 with check!

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/8/3p4/NbP2N2/PP3PPP.text:
Black could also take on b3.

When we recapture with the queen, we activate it and aim at f7. 

We also eye b7 indirectly and clear the d1-square for our rook.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/8/8/NQp2N2/PP3PPP/R.text:
Black could take on c3, but this allows us to play Nb5 with tempo.
 
The black queen now has to stay and guard c7.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/8/8/Nbp2N2/PP2QPPP/.text:
Black could go for this trade. 

We have an interesting in-between move.

The knight on b5 is powerful. It aims at the c7-square for the fork.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnqb3/8/3p4/1BP2N2/PP3PP.text:
Black may offer a trade of bishops. 

Our bishop is more active on b3, so this makes sense.

Bringing our knight out via a3, intending to go to b5, is a dynamic way to play this.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnqb3/8/8/NB3N2/PB2QPPP/.text:
We have a lot of compensation. It won't be easy for Black to hold on to the material. 

We will play Rad1 and Rfe1 to fully maximize our pressure, and Nb5 if Black allows it.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnqb3/8/8/NB3N2/Pp2QPPP/.text:
Black could be greedy and take another pawn. 

They're giving us a big lead in development.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnqb3/8/8/NBp2N2/PP3PPP/.text:
If this capture happens now, we will avoid the queen trade.

We'll go to e2 and prepare Rd1.

r4b1r/pp2pkpp/1nnq4/8/3p2b1/2P2N2/PP3PPP.text:
The king takes.

We give a check. 

This is also a discovered attack on the g4-bishop.

r4bkr/pp2p1pp/1nnq4/6N1/3p2Q1/2P5/PP3PPP.text:
And we recover the piece with some interest: Black's coordination is terrible. 

The king on g8 is vulnerable and prevents the rooks from being connected. If 12...e5, 13. f4 is good. 

White is considerably better.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP1P1P.text:
The move 2...Nf6 is the most popular move in the games of titled players. 

However, under 2000 it is played in only 8% of games.

Now e5 is the most challenging. 

We attack the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2pnP3/8/2P5/PP1P1PPP.text:
3...Ne4 gets the knight trapped with 4. d3, so Nd5 is the best. 

But now we can strengthen the center.

We'll play d4 and connect our pawns.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/3nP3/3p4/2P5/PP3PPP/.text:
Black takes on d4. 

And we won't recapture back right away.

The d-pawn is pinned, so we'll develop a piece with Nf3.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black goes for the Sicilian.

We'll play c3 and go for the Alapin.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
